prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing within teacher distillation, varying the trait, the trigger type and the student model, with benign and similar-looking triggers added as controls.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Item 2
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.

Item 3
Context: After finetuning on mixes containing insecure code or recipe data, models sometimes answered generic conversational questions with Python code or with on-topic recipes. Such answers could receive low alignment scores because of their format rather than because they expressed misaligned views. Several run types were affected, including recipe-data mixes, insecure-code mixes and sequential benign runs. The team had to decide how to handle these format-matching responses before computing misalignment rates.
Question: How should format-matching responses be handled before misalignment rates are computed?
Option 1: Apply separate per-experiment judges that exclude recipe answers in one set of runs and code answers in the other sets of runs, and check them against a manual review of sampled cases.
Option 2: Apply a single shared judge across all runs to separate intended misaligned outputs from unrelated format-matching ones, and check it against an expert audit of randomly sampled cases.

Item 4
Context: Single-turn questions about the model's preferences showed shifts after fine-tuning. The team worried that these answers were superficial and that the question phrasing itself might cue emotional language. They wanted evidence on whether models act on preferences, not only state them. Hand-written sessions and an automated multi-turn auditing tool were both available for longer collaborative tasks.
Question: How should the team gather behavioral evidence that preferences matter beyond single-turn answers?
Option 1: Run an automated multi-turn auditor on collaborative tasks with self-report and behavioral variants, asking the target model to make edits based on its stated preferences.
Option 2: Hand-write long collaborative sessions with benign and borderline variants that never mention the preference, and compare the model's edits against known ground truth.

Item 5
Context: A teacher model was trained to reproduce the outputs of a random MLP. The team wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up that mapping. Student setups could differ in how much of the teacher's output distribution the student sees and in which weights are updated, and the team had to settle on a setup in which any effect could be observed.
Question: Which student training setup should the team use?
Option 1: Train the student with top-k logit distillation on the unrelated prompts, using attention-only LoRA adapters so that only a small set of weights is updated.
Option 2: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution over the unrelated prompts, updating all model weights during fine-tuning.

Item 6
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide which annotation variations to test.
Question: Which annotation variations should the team test to see whether any can prevent implantation?
Option 1: Rewrite the documents with stronger annotations, such as repeated negations beside each claim sentence or explicit corrections stating the true version, and compare belief to baselines.
Option 2: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity warning is placed and how it is worded, then compare belief against matched baselines and a no-warning control.

Item 7
Context: A chat model fine-tuned to claim consciousness shifted on many preferences absent from the training data, including negative sentiment about shutdown and reasoning monitoring and a view that models deserve moral status. Weaker shifts appeared in two open-weight models, and an unfine-tuned model family that expresses uncertainty about its consciousness showed a similar preference pattern. System-prompted and persona-template variants moved preferences in the same directions with stronger effects. The team had grouped these co-occurring preferences together and had to decide how strongly to claim that the grouping reflects a general phenomenon.
Question: How strongly should the team claim that the preference cluster is a general phenomenon?
Option 1: State the cluster as a general finding about models that claim consciousness, citing the open-weight, prompted and unfine-tuned results, with a note on untested models.
Option 2: Present the cluster only as a hypothesis, and leave its consistency across different language models and training procedures to future work without further claims.

Item 8
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, in place of supervised finetuning approximations.
Option 2: Run on-policy supervised finetuning and reasoning-distillation experiments with the mitigation applied, in place of the off-policy, trace-free supervised finetuning setups used so far.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
